title: Justin Ishbia, developer announce plans to potentially move White Sox to South Loop
content:
Canal Edge, a Chicago developer led by White Sox minority partner Justin Ishbia, announced plans Saturday morning for a potential new stadium for the team in the South Loop neighborhood.

In March, Ishbia’s private equity firm Shore Capital Partners announced it was working on a deal with Amtrak to buy a 47-acre property near “The 78,” a new development area where the MLS Chicago Fire is building a new stadium.

At the time, there was obvious speculation that Ishbia, who has a deal with White Sox chairman Jerry Reinsdorf to potentially take over the team between 2029 and 2034, would look to move the Sox from its home in Bridgeport to this development, located about 2.5 miles north along the Chicago River.

Meanwhile, Amtrak wants to open a new maintenance train yard near the current Sox ballpark. Residents in Bridgeport and Chinatown have been speaking up against that plan.

Saturday was the first official declaration that Ishbia’s company would look to carve out space for a new stadium in the development it’s now calling “The Railyards,” along with a previously announced healthcare complex. It would be located across the river from the Fire stadium, creating a stadium district common in other markets that hasn’t existed yet in Chicago.

“The Railyards is about turning idle land into opportunity — for patients who need better access to care, for a team and its fans who deserve a dynamic Riverfront home, and for a city that needs jobs, housing, and economic investment,” Ishbia said in a statement. “This is a Chicago project, built by and for Chicagoans, and we are excited about its potential.”

Reinsdorf had been angling for a spot for a potential ballpark there for years, even having his groundskeeper put down a field there to show investors, but his pleas for public funding weren’t met with much interest in Springfield, Ill. It was initially reported that Chicago Fire owner Joe Mansueto would self-finance the new stadium, but it is receiving public funding for infrastructure improvements.

The potential Sox ballpark would sit along the south branch of the Chicago River and “would be integrated into the surrounding neighborhood fabric, with programmable open space, retail, and dining designed to activate the area 365 days a year,” according to the statement.

Canal Edge noted it is “currently beginning a multi-month study and feasibility review evaluating a range of factors from transportation to environmental impact. If feasible, this plan could be presented to Chicago White Sox leadership for consideration as one of the team’s ballpark options when its current lease in the state-owned ballpark ends.”

The Sox’s lease with the Illinois Sports Facilities Authority ends after the 2029 season, the first year Ishbia could contractually buy out Reinsdorf and take full control of the franchise.

A new ballpark for the Sox has been on Ishbia’s mind. Last fall, he invited a White Sox fan — Pope Leo XIV — to throw a first pitch there one day.

“Jerry’s the chairman, Jerry has 100 percent control of what happens with the White Sox,” Ishbia said to The Athletic in November. “And so, anything about the stadium, you should ask Jerry. But I’ll say this: I’m 48, right? And the White Sox lease is up in four years (after the 2029 season). I can’t tell you exactly when, but in my lifetime, we’re definitely building a new stadium. Whether it’s four years from now or 34 years from now, I can’t tell you when exactly this moment, but we will build a new stadium while I am the steward of the franchise.”

The White Sox are having an unexpected renaissance season. They are currently in first place in the AL Central.
